parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
A piezoelectric transducer containing a quartz crystal is used to obtain diagnostic information about internal structures.

Describe the function of the quartz crystal.

markscheme_points.text: applied p.d. causes crystal to vibrate or vibrations cause crystal to generate an

hints: Hint 1: Think about the two jobs needed for an ultrasound scan - something must send a pulse into the body and something must pick up the echo that comes back.
Hint 2: Remember quartz is piezoelectric, so electrical and mechanical effects are linked in both directions - an applied voltage can cause shape change and a shape change can cause a voltage.
Hint 3: Link high-frequency alternating p.d. to vibration for transmission, and incoming reflected vibrations to an induced e.m.f. for detection.
parts.proper_answer: The crystal acts as both transmitter and receiver. An alternating p.d. applied to the crystal causes it to vibrate at ultrasonic frequency, generating ultrasound. Reflected ultrasound incident on the crystal causes it to vibrate, generating an alternating e.m.f./p.d.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Two-Way Role of the Transducer**
Think of the probe on the skin as doing two jobs in rapid succession. First it must shout, then it must listen. The same quartz crystal does both, switching between transmitting a short pulse of ultrasound and then waiting to receive the weak echoes reflected from internal boundaries.

Step 2: **Transmitting - Electricity to Sound**
Quartz is piezoelectric. When you apply a high-frequency alternating p.d. across it, the crystal expands and contracts at that same frequency. If the driving frequency is above $20 \text{ kHz}$, typically a few $\text{MHz}$, this mechanical vibration generates a pulse of ultrasound that is transmitted into the body: $$\text{alternating p.d.} \rightarrow \text{vibration} \rightarrow \text{ultrasound}$$

Step 3: **Receiving - Sound to Electricity**
The process works in reverse for detection. When reflected ultrasound returns to the probe it forces the crystal to vibrate. Because of the piezoelectric effect this mechanical stress generates an alternating e.m.f. across the crystal, which can be amplified and processed to give information about the depth and nature of the reflecting structure.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the properties of the medium itself, not the wave intensity - one property describes how much mass is packed in, the other describes how fast the ultrasound travels.
Hint 2: Recall how those two quantities are combined by multiplication to give $Z$, with unit $\text{kg m}^{-2} \text{s}^{-1}$.
parts.proper_answer: Specific acoustic impedance $Z$ is the product of the density $\rho$ of the medium and the speed $c$ of ultrasound in the medium, $Z = \rho c$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Impedance Means**
In physics, impedance is a measure of how much a medium resists or controls the passage of a wave. For sound, a dense, stiff medium behaves very differently from a light, soft one.

Step 2: **The Definition**
We define it precisely for the medium as: $$Z = \rho c$$ where $\rho$ is the density of the medium in $\text{kg m}^{-3}$ and $c$ is the speed of ultrasound in that medium in $\text{m s}^{-1}$. So $Z$ has unit $\text{kg m}^{-2} \text{s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Describe, qualitatively, how the specific acoustic impedances of two materials affect the intensity reflection coefficient at a boundary between the materials.

markscheme_points.text: if very different then reflection coe
the lower the difference means lov (any one point)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what causes a strong echo - it is not the absolute value of $Z$ but how much $Z$ changes when the wave meets a boundary.
Hint 2: Compare the two extremes - two very similar soft tissues versus a tissue-air or tissue-bone boundary - and what that means for reflected intensity.
parts.proper_answer: The intensity reflection coefficient depends on the difference between the specific acoustic impedances $Z_1$ and $Z_2$. If $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ are similar, the reflection coefficient is small. If the difference is large, the reflection coefficient is large.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Mismatch Causes Reflection**
When ultrasound meets a boundary, part is transmitted and part is reflected. How much is reflected is governed by how different the two media are acoustically. The formula involves $(Z_1 - Z_2)^2$, so it is the difference or mismatch that matters.

Step 2: **Qualitative Rule**
If the two materials have very similar $Z$ values, for example two types of soft tissue, there is almost no mismatch, most intensity is transmitted and the intensity reflection coefficient is very low. If the $Z$ values are very different, for example soft tissue and air or bone, there is a large mismatch, most intensity is reflected and the intensity reflection coefficient is high. In short, larger difference in $Z$ means larger reflected intensity.
